primaryKeyword: seo for law firms in india
h1: SEO for law firms without tripping Bar Council Rule 36
metaTitle: SEO for Law Firms in India: Rule 36 Safe
metaDescription: SEO for law firms in India that respects Bar Council Rule 36. Practice-area knowledge pages that earn enquiries without reading as solicitation.
answer: Law firm SEO in India works inside Bar Council of India Rule 36, which bars advocates from soliciting work or advertising. A 2008 proviso permits a website carrying your name, address, contact details, enrolment number, qualifications and areas of practice. Everything beyond that has to be knowledge, not promotion.
takeaways: Rule 36 is a **prohibition on solicitation**, not a prohibition on being findable. Publishing the law is not advertising yourself.
The permitted website particulars are narrow and specific. Claims of expertise, case results and testimonials sit outside them.
Your advocates' profile pages are simultaneously the most compliant pages on the site and the strongest credibility signal Google can read.
Paid listings on commercial lawyer-finder portals are the riskiest thing most firms do, and courts have said so.
The 2023–24 replacement of the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act created years of search demand that firms are still not serving properly.

sections.h2: What Rule 36 actually bans — and the proviso most firms have never read
body: Rule 36 sits in the Bar Council of India Rules, in the chapter on standards of professional conduct. In substance it says an advocate shall not solicit work or advertise, directly or indirectly, whether by circulars, advertisements, touts, personal communications, interviews not warranted by personal relations, or by furnishing or inspiring newspaper comments about their cases. The signboard and nameplate must be of reasonable size and must not indicate that the advocate specialises in a particular kind of work or holds office in a bar association.

That reads like a ban on having a website. It isn't. In 2008 the Bar Council added a proviso permitting advocates to furnish specified particulars on their websites, with a declaration filed with the Bar Council and the advocate responsible for the accuracy of what's stated. The permitted list is short, and it is the boundary line for everything else you publish.

So the strategy writes itself. You cannot advertise the lawyer. You can publish the law. Legal search demand is overwhelmingly for the law — what the section says, what the procedure is, how long it takes, what documents are needed. Serve that well and enquiries follow without a single promotional sentence.

callout.title: This is guidance, not an opinion
callout.body: We're an SEO agency, not your ethics counsel. Rule 36 enforcement varies by State Bar Council and the case law keeps moving — courts have recently taken a hard line on advocates advertising through commercial listing portals. Run the content policy past your own compliance partner before you publish, and don't let a marketer decide where the line is.

body: The standard Indian firm website has eight practice-area pages of about 200 words each: "Our corporate law team advises clients across sectors with a client-centric approach." That page cannot rank, because it answers no question, and it is closer to self-promotion than the compliant alternative.

Replace it with a knowledge page. Same URL, same practice area, entirely different content: what the statute says, the procedure step by step, the realistic timeline, the documents, which forum has jurisdiction, and what typically goes wrong. A reader learns something. Nothing on the page claims you are good at it — the page demonstrates it instead, which is the whole point of the rule.
bullets: **Anchor to statute and rule, by section number.** "Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act" is both what people search and the most defensible thing on your site.

**Publish procedure and timeline honestly**, including the delays. "Typically 18–30 months in a metro magistrate's court, longer if service is contested" beats "speedy resolution" on both accuracy and ranking.
**List the documents.** "Documents required for mutual consent divorce" is a real query with high intent and almost no good pages behind it.
**Explain jurisdiction and forum.** NCLT versus DRT versus civil court, consumer commission pecuniary limits, which High Court hears what. Genuinely confusing, genuinely searched.
**Update when the law changes.** A page describing pre-2024 criminal procedure is now wrong, and wrong is a bigger reputational risk for a firm than invisible.

sections.h2: Advocate profiles: your safest pages and your strongest signal
body: Every particular the 2008 proviso permits is also, conveniently, an [E-E-A-T](/glossary/e-e-a-t) signal. Name, enrolment number, State Bar Council, qualifications, areas of practice. That is a verifiable professional identity, published as text, on a page search engines can resolve to a real person.

Build one properly for every advocate in the firm and link each one from the practice-area pages they work on. Author bylines on knowledge pages should point to those profiles. It costs a week and it does more for credibility than a year of blog posts by "Admin".
bullets: Enrolment number and the Bar Council of enrolment. It's permitted, it's verifiable, and almost nobody publishes it.
Degrees, university, year. Bar admissions and any additional qualifications — CS, CA, patent agent registration, a foreign bar.
Courts and tribunals where the advocate appears, stated as fact.
Publications, journal articles, lectures and teaching posts. This is where credibility legitimately accumulates without describing results.
Languages of practice. In India this is a real filter for a client and almost never mentioned.

callout.title: Reported judgments: handle carefully
callout.body: Judgments are public record, and there's a strong pull to list the ones your advocates argued. Understand what that page is doing, though: a list of wins is a claim about results, which is exactly what Rule 36 restricts. The conservative version — publishing case commentary on judgments regardless of who appeared — carries the same credibility with far less risk.

sections.h2: Directories, listings and the map pack
body: This is where firms get into trouble, usually because someone sold them a package. Paid placements on commercial lawyer-finder portals — the "top 10 divorce lawyers in your city" pages — are advertising by any reading, and Indian courts have recently directed Bar Councils to act against advocates who use them. A [paid list placement isn't a ranking](/journal/why-best-seo-agency-lists-are-paid), it's an ad with an editorial costume on.

The map pack is a subtler question. A Google Business Profile carrying the firm's name, address, hours and phone number is factual information of the sort the proviso already contemplates for a website. Where it gets uncomfortable is category selection that signals specialisation, and soliciting client reviews — which raises both Rule 36 and confidentiality problems in one move. The conservative path is a factual listing, a general category, and no review campaign. Discuss it with your own compliance partner rather than treating [local SEO](/services/local-seo-services) as a default.
bullets: **Keep name, address and phone identical everywhere.** Inconsistent details across listings weaken the entity signal and confuse clients equally.
**Free factual entries in bar association and directory listings** are a different animal from a paid "featured" slot. Know which one you've been sold.
**Never solicit or reply to reviews with case detail.** A grateful client naming their matter in a public review is a confidentiality breach you invited.
**One office, one page, staffed.** Firms with three offices need three pages with real addresses and real people, not fifteen city pages targeting cities they don't sit in.

sections.h2: The queries you can serve without soliciting anything
body: Legal search in India runs enormous volumes and is served mostly by aggregator content farms and outdated blog posts. A firm that writes accurately about its own practice areas has a structural advantage: the pages are right, and correctness is checkable.

The single largest opening right now is the criminal law overhaul. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act from 1 July 2024. Every practitioner, student, HR team and journalist in the country is still translating section numbers between the old code and the new. That demand runs for years and most of what ranks for it is thin.

sections.h2: Enquiry handling, pricing and what we'll actually promise
body: The last place firms slip is the form. "Get your free consultation now" is an inducement. "Talk to our expert" is a claim of specialisation. Both undo a compliant site in six words. Label it "Enquiry", state what happens next and how long it takes, note that no attorney-client relationship arises from the form, and run a conflict check before anyone replies with substance.

Measure by practice area, not by sessions. The only report worth reading maps query to page to enquiry to matter opened. A criminal law page generating fifty enquiries a month that your firm can't take on is a cost, not a win.

Our SEO runs from ₹75,000/mo, and from ₹40,000/mo for smaller sites — ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, 30 days' notice, and you keep every asset. Details on [our pricing page](/pricing).

What we commit to is not a ranking position. Nobody controls Google's index, and a firm should be more sceptical of that promise than most. We freeze your trailing-90-day qualified enquiries from organic search on day one, and if we haven't beaten that number in 90 days we keep working free until we do.

callout.title: The agency red flag specific to your profession
callout.body: If an SEO pitch includes "best lawyer in [city]" as a target keyword, a testimonials page, or a paid directory package, walk out. They have written the same deck for a dentist and swapped the nouns — and the professional consequences land on you, not on them.

faqs.q: Can Indian law firms legally do SEO at all?
faqs.a: Yes. Rule 36 restricts solicitation and advertising, not being findable. A website carrying the permitted particulars plus genuine legal knowledge is compliant, and ranking that content is a consequence of it being useful. What's restricted is claims about your ability, results, testimonials and paid promotion.

faqs.q: What can a law firm website include under Rule 36?
faqs.a: The 2008 proviso permits name, address, telephone numbers and email, enrolment number and Bar Council, professional and academic qualifications, and areas of practice — with a declaration filed with the Bar Council and the advocate answerable for accuracy. Most firms add an informational disclaimer confirming no solicitation is intended.

faqs.q: Are paid listings on lawyer directories allowed?
faqs.a: Paid placements are the riskiest thing most firms do online. Courts in India have directed Bar Councils to act against advocates advertising through commercial listing portals. A free factual entry is a different proposition from a paid featured slot — know which one your marketing budget bought.

faqs.q: Should a law firm ask clients for Google reviews?
faqs.a: We'd advise against a review campaign. Soliciting testimonials sits close to the solicitation Rule 36 restricts, and a client describing their matter publicly creates a confidentiality problem you invited. Take the ranking hit; it's smaller than the professional exposure.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to bring a law firm enquiries?
faqs.a: Procedure and statute-mapping pages on an established domain often gather impressions within six to ten weeks because the competing content is thin. Competitive commercial terms — corporate, arbitration, IP in a metro — take six to twelve months. The range reflects domain age and how much of the existing site has to be rewritten first.

faqs.q: Is legal content written by AI a problem for a firm?
faqs.a: A serious one. Generated legal content confidently cites sections that don't exist and misses amendments — and after the 2024 criminal law replacement, most training data describes a code that's been repealed. Every page should be reviewed and signed by an advocate before it goes live, which is also what makes it rankable.
